timeline.event: W. E. Cooke reported fibrosis of the lungs due to inhalation of asbestos dust in the British Medical Journal, an early clinical description of asbestosis.
Richard Doll reported excess lung cancer mortality among asbestos workers.
Wagner, Sleggs and Marchand described 33 cases of diffuse pleural mesothelioma in South Africa, all but one with probable exposure to crocidolite.
Selikoff, Churg and Hammond linked asbestos exposure among insulation workers to lung cancer, mesothelioma and other neoplasms.
EPA issued the Asbestos Ban and Phase-out Rule under TSCA in July; in 1991 the Fifth Circuit vacated most of it in Corrosion Proof Fittings v. EPA, 947 F.2d 1201.
Commission Directive 1999/77/EC required EU member states to ban the use of chrysotile asbestos by 1 January 2005, with a limited exception for existing electrolysis diaphragms.
Directive (EU) 2023/2668 lowered the EU occupational exposure limit to 2,000 fibres/m3, counting fibres 0.2 to 3 micrometers wide.
EPA published its Part 1 chrysotile asbestos rule under TSCA section 6 on 28 March, banning the remaining known ongoing uses with phased compliance dates.

timeline.event: A study spun 100% cotton ring yarns containing recycled pre- and post-consumer fiber, reaching about 25% recycled content in 30 Ne yarn.
A cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment compared fabrics with 30% mechanically recycled cotton against 100% virgin cotton.
The Swedish cotton-to-pulp recycler Renewcell, whose pulp was sold as Circulose, was bought out of bankruptcy by the investment firm Altor.
Textile Exchange estimated recycled cotton at about 0.3 million tonnes, roughly 1% of cotton production.
Rotor yarns blending upcycled waste with cotton were assessed for quality.

production.scope: global recycled cotton, pre- and post-consumer

timeline.event: Aquafil began chemically regenerating nylon 6 waste in Ljubljana, Slovenia, under the ECONYL name, according to the producer.
A screening study characterized natural enzymes able to depolymerize nylon 6.
Recycled polyamide made up about 2% of polyamide fiber, roughly 0.2 million tonnes.
A life cycle assessment of nylon 6 remonomerization found the alkaline route cut global warming potential by about 80% relative to fossil caprolactam.

timeline.event: Courtaulds petitioned the FTC for a new generic fiber name so that the fiber need not be labeled rayon.
The FTC approved lyocell as a name for fabric content labeling.
Lenzing acquired the Tencel Group, including plants at Mobile, Alabama, and Grimsby, England.
Lenzing introduced TENCEL lyocell with REFIBRA technology, containing recycled cotton pulp.

timeline.event: Lenzing launched LENZING ECOVERO viscose, reporting that it carried the EU Ecolabel (license AT/016/001) at launch.
Trade press reported that Lenzing paired the launch with fiber identification technology intended to let buyers trace ECOVERO in finished goods.

timeline.event: Aquafil expanded into Slovenia through the privatization of a former state company.
Aquafil began pursuing a full waste-to-yarn regeneration loop for nylon 6.
Aquafil launched the ECONYL Regeneration System, with depolymerization to caprolactam and repolymerization at Ljubljana, Slovenia.
Aquafil published an Environmental Product Declaration for ECONYL nylon textile filament yarns.
